It was more than just celibacy; the Shakers designed their homes, their places of worship, and their lives to limit and police any interaction between men and women. The sexes were equal in value and authority, but they intermingled only during their ecstatic worship services. Mother Ann Lee had a truly devastating experience with marriage. It appears that she never loved or chose her husband; the marriage may have been arranged by her family. All four of her children died, and she suffered permanent physical damage from childbirth. I grew up in Paris and left France when I was 25. I married a U.S. Air Force captain, lived in Germany for four years, and eventually moved to America.

Having experienced both sides, I can tell you that French and American cultures are remarkably different. I have often felt that the French have a deeply ingrained culture of discontent, with a tendency to depend heavily on the state for just about everything. France offers tremendous social benefits, and these come at a considerable cost.

In America, a much more capitalist society, the mentality is quite different. You are expected to fight for a job, work hard, and take responsibility for much more of your own well-being.

In France, the social system provides paid sick leave, maternity leave, and numerous other benefits. Healthcare is largely funded through social contributions and taxes. Of course, these benefits are not free; ultimately, taxpayers finance them, including the very people who rely on them.

In America, the philosophy is almost the opposite. Many Americans would rather keep more of their earnings than pay higher taxes upfront to finance a comprehensive social system. Healthcare, dental care, vision insurance, and much of one’s personal safety net are individual responsibilities, often requiring separate insurance policies and out-of-pocket payments.

Neither system is without its shortcomings, and both come with advantages and disadvantages. 2 very different philosophies and ways of life.

It's tempting to jump into the public versus charter fight.

But it's more practical to review the third option - to bring back small public theme schools, like the former community school district 4 schools of choice in East Harlem.

Founded 50 years ago - East Harlem’s District 4 schools of choice transformed large, failing public schools into three or four smaller schools inside the same building to give every child individualized attention. The model propelled the district from dead last in New York City, where just 15% of students read at grade level, to 63%, matching the citywide reading average within 14 years and reaching over 90% of the city average in math, before Schools Chancellor Joel Klein dismantled the system in 2003.

There's a public model that works - a model that achieves that is backed by data - use it.

If you need pointers instead of recreating the wheel - one of the greatest education leaders I know, former CSD 4 superintendent, Evelyn Castro, is in higher education leadership at Medgar Evers college. Talk with her, please.

It’s an odd story. The LW’s friend is the one who has (or had) the substantive proof of the cheating, so why does she need the LW to be involved? Is she embarrassed that she helped the cheater cheat, either through her participation or coverup?

​Built on a modular stainless steel frame, the RTS was engineered like a tank compared to a lot of the lighter low-floor buses that came later. Between the durability of the body, the independent front suspension that handled potholes far better than older solid-axle coaches, and the distinct growl of the Detroit Diesel engines—especially the two-stroke 6V92TA—they had a presence and a toughness that modern buses rarely match.

​Even as the MTA finally retired the last of the Nova Bus RTS fleet a few years ago in 2019, operators, mechanics, and riders alike still point to them as the gold standard for reliability and heavy-duty transit design. They truly don't build them like that anymore.

I worked for Dick in one of my first jobs out of art school. He could be vicious and then incredibly generous within minutes, and he often scared the hell out of me.

I was a kid who loved to make things, entering a world where who you knew could matter more than what you could do, or how well you could do it. That world was foreign to me. It still is. Outsized personalities are a dime a dozen, and proximity to money, beauty or privilege can buy someone a convincing appearance of significance.

Dick’s commercial success gave him extraordinary access- but he did so much more with it than anyone I've encountered since. He got to know people. He spent hours on the phone, went to the theater, read whenever he was alone (he was rarely alone). He was always looking, talking, divining; trying to understand what made someone compelling. It wasn’t conventional beauty. He could bring something out of a person that I doubt they knew they possessed.

His whole personality was theater, but his curiosity was authentic. He wasn’t collecting people as credentials. He wanted to discover what was inside them.

He cared deeply about being recognized as an artist, at a time when the boundary between art and commercial photography was firmly drawn. Yet his way of living and working helped create the intersections of art, fashion and culture that now seem inseparable.

Dick was no enigma. He was a life made brighter next to someone else.

comments.name: DG
comments.body: From teaching classes in how people learn, I can write a little something about learning curves and magic. H. Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences says there are eight categories of knowing and doing. The intelligences are (a) verbal, (b) quantitative (math), (c) musical (yes, it is independent), (d) naturalistic (good w/plants & animals), (e) intrapersonal (knowing about oneself), (f) interpersonal (good with others), (g) spatial-visual (good with shapes etc.), and (h) kinesthetic (dancing, athletics). Everybody has different learning speeds at each of these. There is no immediate "talent' nor surefire failure in anyone. Magicians, I'd say, generally have fast natural learning curves at the last three. Me, I'm a really slow learner kinesthetically; it'd take me a long, long time to perform a trick smoothly. Maybe Ms. Egan is a bit like me. But I'm a quick learner, and I bet she is too, at interpersonal intelligence, at communication: Look how well she writes, so skillfully leading the reader along. Which is what magicians do: They lead us along. It's like magic.

I believe things happen for a reason, and there is no point in worrying about things we cannot control. Bad luck is just a belief. I think people follow superstitions because they feel like it gives them control over situations they cannot predict. However, I think it is better to focus on what is actually happening instead of worrying about signs or unlucky things. Personally, I just spend my day normally, even on Friday the 13th.

comments.name: Adelyn F
comments.body: I think everyone has at least one superstition, even if they do not fully believe in them. One superstition I know is that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck. Another common superstition is knocking on wood to avoid bad luck. Personally, I do not believe superstitions can control what happens in my life, but I still sometimes follow them just in case. I think people follow superstitions because they make them feel more comfortable and give them a sense of control. Other common superstitions include walking under a ladder, opening an umbrella inside, and having a black cat cross your path. Even though there is no proof these things cause bad luck, many people still avoid them. I also think superstitions are interesting because they are passed down through families and generations. Parents might teach their children superstitions they learned from their own parents. Over time, these beliefs become traditions. I think superstitions can also be fun because they give people something to talk about. Even if someone does not believe in them, they might still knock on wood just to be safe. Overall, I think superstitions are more about personal beliefs and traditions than facts. I may not believe they can change my luck, but I still think they are interesting and fun to follow.

Today, I did do something different and went to the gym, but I don't think that counts. I'm not that superstitious. For example, I don't believe 7 is a lucky number, or 13 is particularly bad. However, I do believe that your Zodiac influences who you are. Not in the most powerful way, and I know that the month you're born in has nothing to do with your personality, but I just feel that it impacts you in some way. I think superstitions are just a waste of your fear and anxiety. A superstition that I do follow is that before every sports game or swim meet, I don't jinx it. I can't talk about the game before or during, and I really don't like it when teammates congratulate me too much. I stick with it because whenever I do it, I do pretty well. However, I think just writing this is jinxing it. I think people might participate in rituals or beliefs that don't necessarily make sense because it gives them a sense of control. And people really like to be in control, so that's probably why people follow these superstitions.
